articles.summary: Armenia–Russia Relations: Toward Confrontation or Dialogue?  MassisPost
articles.full_text:
By KRIKOR KHODANIAN
Relations between the Republic of Armenia and the Russian Federation have entered a difficult and tense period. The two countries, once allies, are now deeply divided over how to reassess the past and shape their future relationship.
The 44-day war and the events that followed—particularly Russia’s indifference when Azerbaijani forces invaded Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2022, followed by its abandonment of the Armenians of Artsakh, whom it had been entrusted to protect—have left Armenians deeply disillusioned. This disappointment will be difficult to overcome in the foreseeable future.
Yerevan is seeking to redefine its future relations with Moscow on a new basis, with Armenia’s national and state interests serving as the guiding principles. Moscow, however, maintains that the former ties should be restored and that the two countries should remain loyal allies and partners in all fields, including the economy, politics, defense, and other areas.
Senior Russian officials continue to oppose Armenia’s foreign policy of closer ties with European countries, issuing warnings at times and threats at others. Among the latest was a statement by Dmitry Medvedev, Russia’s former president and current deputy chairman of its Security Council, who warned that Armenia could become “the new Ukraine.”
“Armenia’s current leadership has decided to change the direction of its development. I am confident that this will lead to nothing good. The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is its transformation into a new Ukraine,” he said.
Since the war in Ukraine began, Medvedev has effectively been tasked with delivering some of the most extreme statements directed against the West. He has repeatedly threatened the use of nuclear weapons as a means of bringing the war to an end. His latest remarks directed at Armenia should therefore be viewed in this broader context.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan described Medvedev’s comments as incomprehensible, adding:
“Armenia has already faced such a danger and found itself in a similar situation when the CSTO failed to fulfill its obligations toward Armenia. Why is Mr. Medvedev making such a statement? One could just as easily make a statement warning that Armenia might suddenly turn into a new Russia, given that explosions are occurring in various parts of Russia. This is not a good genre.”
Despite the accusations coming from the Kremlin, Yerevan is trying to avoid a complete rupture in relations with Moscow, seeking to resolve existing disagreements on the basis of mutual respect.
Thanks to these efforts, contacts between the leaders of the two countries, which had been interrupted for a period following Armenia’s parliamentary elections, have resumed. Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Vladimir Putin have held several bilateral meetings and telephone conversations on the sidelines of international summits, seeking common ground on outstanding issues.
Until recently, Pashinyan had stated that Armenia needed small modular nuclear power plants that could be built by American companies. He has since changed his position, arguing that the construction of a large nuclear power plant would be more appropriate, while leaving open the possibility of entrusting the project to Russian companies. In this way, Yerevan appears to be signaling that it is not constrained by its differences with Moscow and remains willing to continue cooperating with Russia.
Several outstanding issues remain to be resolved, the most important of which concerns the management of Armenia’s railway network. Yerevan believes that control of the network should be transferred from the Russian company currently operating it to a company from another country, allowing Armenia’s railways to connect with regional transportation networks. Otherwise, Armenia risks being excluded from new projects because of the sanctions imposed on Russian companies.
Moscow firmly rejects this proposal. Is Yerevan raising the possibility of entrusting the construction of a nuclear power plant to Russian companies in an attempt to soften Moscow’s position on railway management? The answer may become clear in the coming months.
Negotiations on gas supplies are also expected in December. During these talks, Russia may demand a price increase, arguing that Armenia currently benefits from discounted gas prices as a member of the Eurasian Economic Union. However, if Armenia has chosen the path toward European Union membership, Russia may argue that it should pay international market prices, which are several times higher.
Russia has recently unveiled a new initiative dubbed the “Putin Route.” The project aims to connect Russia, Georgia, and Armenia through the construction of roads and railways running through Abkhazia. The initiative is viewed as a geopolitical response to the “Trump Route,” which passes through Armenia and has already begun moving toward implementation.
Armenia–Russia relations thus face new tests and challenges that must be addressed with composure and pragmatism. At every turn, Armenia has demonstrated its willingness to engage in sincere and constructive dialogue. The remaining question is whether the Russian side will demonstrate the same willingness.

articles.title: Congress Passed Its Most Sweeping Russia Sanctions in Years. Trump Shelved Them Before They Took Effect - Latin Times
articles.summary: Congress Passed Its Most Sweeping Russia Sanctions in Years. Trump Shelved Them Before They Took Effect  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Just 28 days after signing what lawmakers called the most expansive Russia sanctions legislation Congress had ever produced, President Donald Trump issued an executive order on October 16 suspending virtually the entire package — two days before it was set to take effect.
The move effectively neutralized a law named in honor of a recently deceased Republican senator, giving the White House far wider latitude over sanctions policy while blocking all new statutory penalties from activating.
A Bipartisan Blockbuster That Moved in Stages
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 advanced through both chambers of Congress in successive steps. The Senate acted first: on August 7, 2026, the upper chamber approved the measure 86–11, with only 10 Democratic senators and Republican Rand Paul voting against it, while three Republicans did not vote. The bill then moved to the House, which agreed to the Senate's amended version on September 16 by a vote of 262–159, with 58 Democrats and 203 Republicans voting in favor, along with one independent. Seven House Republicans joined most Democrats in opposition.
Trump signed the act into law on September 18, 2026. The legislation codified and expanded existing U.S. sanctions against Russia, broadened authorities to designate individuals for secondary sanctions, introduced steep new tariff powers with a particular focus on Russian energy exports, and extended the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 by five years, through 2031.
Named for a Senator Who Championed It Until His Final Days
The law bears the name of the late Senator Lindsey Graham (R-SC), who co-introduced earlier versions of the bill with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut beginning in April 2025 and who spent more than a year building support — at one point counting 84 Senate co-sponsors before the legislation reached a floor vote. A final agreement with the White House on the bill's terms was reached in the days immediately before Graham's death. Graham died on July 11, 2026, from what his office described as a brief and sudden illness — the night after returning from his tenth wartime visit to Kyiv, where he had met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
After Graham's death, his sister Darline Graham Nordone was appointed to his Senate seat and became the legislation's lead Senate sponsor through its passage. The House cleared the bill roughly two months after Graham's death.
What the Law Was Built to Do
The Graham Act was structured as a multi-layered economic squeeze on Russia's war financing. Section 112 authorized duties of up to 500 percent ad valorem on all Russian imports, stacked on top of any existing tariffs. Section 113 established that the five countries purchasing the largest volumes of Russian crude oil or natural gas — and making new purchases after October 18, the implementation date — could face tariffs of up to 100 percent on all their exports to the United States, irrespective of whether individual shipments complied with the Western price cap on Russian oil. That provision put China and India squarely in the crosshairs, as both rank among Moscow's largest energy customers.
The act also codified existing sanctions imposed under Executive Order 14024 and required sanctions on the Central Bank of Russia, Sberbank, VTB Bank, Gazprombank, and other state-controlled financial institutions and their subsidiaries. It further targeted Russia's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing restrictions, and foreign firms supporting Russia's defense industry.
What Trump Actually Signed on October 16
Trump's executive order does not repeal the Graham Act, but it suspends all of its new punitive provisions. The order waives the 500 percent tariff increase on Russian goods under Section 112, the 100 percent tariff on the top five importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas under Section 113, and the 100 percent tariff on the top five countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion. It also waives the sanctions on designated foreign persons under multiple sections of the law.
The order preserves all Russia sanctions that were already in place under prior executive orders before the Graham Act became law — but none of the new statutory measures enter into force.
Trump invoked Section 115 of the act, which authorizes him to waive any provision by submitting to Congress a written certification that doing so is in the national interest of the United States. The certification was submitted, but the order gave the administration much wider latitude going forward to decide which sanctions to keep in place without being legally bound by the act's requirements. The waiver contains no expiration date.
Fuel Prices and the Iran War Factor
The timing of the waiver is closely tied to the Trump administration's push to lower domestic fuel prices, which have climbed in connection with the ongoing U.S. conflict with Iran. The move came after Trump announced a separate deal last week allowing Russia to resume diesel exports to U.S. and global markets, with Moscow pledging to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel. By waiving the secondary tariff provisions, the president also avoided forcing China and India to choose between continued Russian energy purchases and access to American markets — a pressure campaign that proponents had billed as one of the law's most potent geopolitical tools.
Zelenskyy Condemns the Decision
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was swift to respond after the waiver was announced. His remarks came just two days after Russia launched a massive missile and drone strike on October 14 against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, damaging equipment at 26 energy sector sites and four oil and gas facilities, leaving hundreds of thousands of people without power. Zelenskyy had in the preceding weeks repeatedly called on Trump to enforce the Graham Act, telling visiting U.S. lawmakers in Kyiv on October 9 that Ukraine was counting on the legislation being fully implemented. After the waiver, Zelenskyy posted on X criticizing the decision as undermining meaningful pressure on Moscow at a critical moment in the war.
Congressional Backlash Crosses Party Lines
Criticism in Washington was not limited to Democrats. A group of roughly a dozen Republican senators — including Mitch McConnell, Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, John Cornyn, and Alan Armstrong — had urged Trump just days before to rescind the Russian diesel agreement and implement the sanctions required by law. Senator Richard Blumenthal, the Connecticut Democrat who co-authored the legislation with Graham, publicly condemned the waiver. Several House Democrats issued statements characterizing the waiver as an abandonment of the policy tools Congress had just handed the president.
A bipartisan group from the Congressional Ukraine Caucus — representatives Marcy Kaptur, Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike Quigley, and Joe Wilson — had written to Trump in late September calling on him not to ease sanctions against Russia, arguing that doing so would only embolden the Kremlin and prolong the war, and urging him to impose the first round of sanctions designations under the Graham Act ahead of the October 18 deadline.
The Escape Hatch That Was Always There
Legal analysts noted that the presidential waiver built into the Graham Act was not an afterthought — it was a condition the White House insisted on before agreeing to support the bill. Section 115 gives the president authority to suspend any provision by certifying to Congress that the waiver is in the national interest. Section 117 of the act also delegates ongoing monitoring authority to the U.S. Trade Representative, who must track Russian energy purchase volumes and sanctions evasion activity and report to the president — preserving the administration's option to reimpose tariffs at any point if it reverses course.
For measures relating to Russia specifically, termination of the act's core provisions would generally require the president to certify that Russia has signed a peace agreement accepted by Ukraine and has ceased military hostilities. No such certification has been submitted.
For now, the most expansive Russia sanctions package Congress has ever passed sits dormant, its provisions indefinitely suspended by the same president who signed it into law less than a month before.

articles.title: The Incentives Of Incomplete Victory: Russia’s Geoeconomic War Engine – OpEd - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: The Incentives Of Incomplete Victory: Russia’s Geoeconomic War Engine – OpEd  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The article argues that Russia’s prolonged campaign cannot be explained solely by battlefield failure, citing incentives such as expanded state control over the economy through nationalizations valued at roughly 6.5 trillion rubles and sustained hydrocarbon revenues amid high oil prices.
- It notes that sanctions failed to collapse the economy, that wartime conditions have delayed Ukrainian elections under martial law, and that demobilizing hundreds of thousands of combatants poses reintegration risks inside Russia.
- The piece concludes that partnerships with China, Iran, India, North Korea, and Belarus, together with redirected energy sales, have created economic and strategic reasons for Moscow to continue the conflict even while both sides incur heavy costs.
When the Russian army entered Ukraine, a lot of propaganda was flying around, purporting that Russian President Vladimir Putin and his military brass had plans to overrun the whole of Ukraine in just three days.
This claim is disputed, but it was common to expect that at this stage the so-called special military operation (SMO) that Russia started on Feb. 24, 2022, would have ended. Yet more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, the war remains unresolved, raising a fundamental question: Why has Moscow continued to sustain such a costly campaign rather than seek an outright military settlement?
Meanwhile, analytical evidence is growing in great numbers that points to why Russia is still heavily invested in its SMO in Ukraine; that is to say, why Russia has not won or concluded it on a decisive and favorable military footing.
Unequivocally, Ukraine has demonstrated significant battlefield adaptation and innovation since the full-scale invasion, particularly in its use of drones and other emerging technologies. That is why Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was touring the Gulf and Arab nations, pitching drone and military cooperation between their armed forces and Ukraine’s.
But it is also worth remembering that there are incentives for Putin not to go all out in Ukraine seeking to upend the country, and for his armed forces not to have intensively and exhaustively sought a comprehensive battlefield victory or an end to the SMO. They include the following.
The war has substantially expanded the Russian state’s intervention in the economy, strengthening the Kremlin’s control over strategic industries and redirecting production toward military Keynesianism. The economy is now strategically steered away from the powerful oligarchs who were once the master key to propelling it forward.
When Putin became president, the Russian economy was in tatters, a default-ridden inheritance from 1998. Putin then presided over a decade of commodity-driven stabilization.
For instance, Russia’s gross domestic product shrank by roughly 40% to 50% over the decade before Putin became president, and in August 1998 the Russian government defaulted on its domestic debt (GKOs) and devalued the ruble.
Meanwhile, after he became president, the Russian economy achieved an extraordinary average GDP growth rate of roughly 7% annually, while real GDP grew by 83% to 94% over this period. Nominal GDP surged from $195.9 billion to more than $1.66 trillion. External debt dropped from 1,243% of foreign reserves to just 8.9%, bringing massive fiscal stability.
Russian citizens also experienced a monumental rise in purchasing power. Real wages grew more than 10% annually, resulting in a 340% overall gain in real wages and a 280% increase in pensions.
But just after the invasion, the Russian economy sharply declined and contracted, because the Western response to the invasion was designed to trigger a systemic banking collapse by freezing roughly $300 billion of Russia’s foreign currency reserves and severing major Russian banks from the SWIFT network. Freezing roughly $300 billion in reserves was an enormous financial shock, but it did not return Russia’s economy to 1998 conditions. It was a rapid decoupling of a G20 economy from Western financial systems and institutions.
Because the initial sanctions carved out exemptions for oil and gas deliveries to Europe, a massive surge in global commodity prices generated record windfalls. Russia banked a record $227 billion current account surplus in 2022, artificially propping up the ruble and absorbing the shock of corporate departures.
When the war started, Western governments led by the United States unleashed a hailstorm of sanctions that were primed to cripple the Russian economy and tank the ruble. After some months of ripple effects, including high ruble liquidity, an unstable economy and the disappearance of both essential and nonessential goods from shop counters in Russia, Western news lines were, at least at that moment, filled with promising notes about the imminent decay of the Russian economy.
But the war, coupled with the U.S.-Israel-Iran war and now the Houthi-Yemen-Saudi Arabia war, is making oil costly. The difficulty of buying oil for industrial and domestic use has helped to raise the much-needed funds to put the Russian economy on full growth throttle and to finance the army, the navy and the Aerospace Forces (VKS) appropriately.
Because bulk carriers and tanker ships risk being struck by missiles or sea mines when transiting the Strait of Hormuz, even when U.S. military vessels escort them, global insurance for ships willing to risk such transits alongside the U.S. military has fallen tremendously, further skyrocketing the price of oil.
The Houthis have demonstrated an ability to threaten commercial shipping around the Bab al-Mandab, increasing the security risks associated with one of the world’s major maritime chokepoints and further tightening the noose on global oil markets and supplies.
These energy weaponization tactics, coupled with Iranian and Houthi conflicts around major maritime chokepoints, increase supply risk and insurance costs, potentially supporting higher oil prices and thereby improving the revenue environment for major exporters such as Russia. They also raise Middle Eastern supply chain vulnerability and the risks of transit.
Russian crude (such as Urals) gained a massive competitive edge, not because the Gulf closed entirely, but because high maritime insurance and Red Sea risk surcharges forced global refiners, especially in China and India, to heavily prioritize discount-priced, shadow-tanker-delivered Russian energy.
Meanwhile, the Russian government now temporarily controls or has nationalized important manufacturing hubs and companies inside Russia, taking them from their Western owners and even from Russian elites or oligarchs.
This has helped the Russian government under Putin provide jobs and employment opportunities to Russian citizens at almost no cost. The state could acquire existing productive capacity without bearing the full historical cost of building it from scratch. Rather than building industrial capacity from the ground up, it acquired fully equipped, turn-key manufacturing hubs at minimal capital cost.
For instance, the Russian government has nationalized or placed several companies under temporary state management, including Fortum Oyj, Uniper, Danone, Carlsberg Group, Wintershall Dea, OMV, Glavprodukt, Toyota, Renault and Achema. These nationalizations and temporary state administrations have transferred an estimated 6.5 trillion rubles (about $89.7 billion) worth of private and foreign assets to the Russian government.
Legal and economic reports say the total value of the seized private and foreign assets is roughly equivalent to Russia’s annual budget deficit, or about one-third of its annual military expenditures.
Also, when massive firms like Danone Russia or Carlsberg’s Baltika Breweries were placed under “temporary management,” their combined workforces, totaling tens of thousands of employees, simply kept working at the same factories under new, state-appointed bosses. This ability to retain workforces, effectively avoiding massive retrenchment and layoffs, cemented Putin’s image as an economic guru and critically acted as a stabilizer to his approval rating, which started to plummet at the inception of the SMO.
But then, the war has successfully created a “rally round the flag” effect by keeping the average Ukrainian preoccupied with war efforts. The continuation of martial law has created political consequences for Kyiv: Presidential elections cannot be held under the existing legal framework, meaning Zelenskyy’s wartime presidency has continued beyond the normal electoral timetable. In so doing, the war continues and the Russian government reaps bountiful sales from hydrocarbons.
Meanwhile, in Russia, demobilizing hundreds of thousands of battle-hardened combatants presents a formidable reintegration and security challenge for the post-war state. Remember, Russia recruited prisoners, especially through Wagner, who were pardoned and declared state heroes, so they cannot be jailed again when they return.
If they were back and idle, imagine the skill of these battle-hardened soldiers if they chose violence over peace and became armed robbers or extremists instead of taking up 9-to-5 jobs. This would effectively bring the Russian Federation back to the post-Chechen war era, when insurgencies were paramount, and Putin wouldn’t want that, considering that Russians idolize him for the calmness and security he has been able to provide and maintain.

articles.title: Russia-Azerbaijan Economic Discussions Put 2026 Trade, Investment & Logistics In Focus: Analysis - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: Russia-Azerbaijan Economic Discussions Put 2026 Trade, Investment & Logistics In Focus: Analysis  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
Trade between Azerbaijan and Russia amounted to US$2.411 billion in January-August 2026, nearly 1.4 times less than in the same period last year, according to data from Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee. The 2026 Russia-Azerbaijan trade decline in 8M follows previous increases. Russia-Azerbaijan trade totaled US$4.92 billion in 2025, an increase of 2.5% from 2024, while Russia ranked as Azerbaijan’s third-largest foreign-trade partner after Italy and Turkiye, accounting for 9.96% of Azerbaijan’s total foreign trade. Azerbaijan exported US$1.184 billion in goods to Russia and imported US$3.736 billion from the Russian market.
The decline is down to political disputes, accelerated by an unfortunate aviation incident, in addition to Azerbaijan’s wariness to trade with Russia and incur secondary sanctions. On the other hand, it also shows that the door is open if Russian exporters want to take up the challenge. Both countries are members of the Commonwealth of Independent States, meaning the supporting trade mechanism exists.
Political and diplomatic ties between Moscow and Baku reached multi-year lows following geopolitical shifts, including the December 2024 accidental downing of an Azerbaijani plane by Russian air defense, disputes over Karabakh and Russian peacekeepers, and the detention of Azerbaijani diaspora members in Yekaterinburg in 2025.
These political tensions spilled over into economic and administrative friction, with mutual crackdowns, stricter customs or agricultural constraints, and the suspension or stalling of major joint economic projects and bilateral negotiations.
Baku has increasingly distanced itself from dependence on Moscow, deepening strategic, energy, and defense ties with Western nations such as the United States and United Kingdom, Turkiye, and Israel, while independently managing its regional logistics and transit corridors such as the INSTC Middle Corridor. These are the obstacles that need to be overcome to get the mutual trade flows back on track.
The 2024 figures show the scale of Russia’s role as a supplier and the opportunity to strengthen Azerbaijani exports in return. Agriculture remained one of the strongest areas of two-way trade. Russia purchased more than US$1.174 billion in Azerbaijani non-oil products in 2025, including agricultural exports worth more than US$837 million. Fruit and vegetable shipments alone reached US$696 million, nearly 31% above the previous year. Azerbaijan exported 700,600 tons of fruit and vegetables to Russia in 2025, compared with 594,800 tons in 2024, an increase of 17.8%.
The momentum continued in several product categories during early 2026. Russia’s onion imports from Azerbaijan increased 1,130%, strawberry imports rose 330%, potato imports grew 41.9% and pear imports increased 37.4%. By May 8, Russia had received 3,900 tons of Azerbaijani fish and seafood, 43% more than a year earlier. Russian agricultural supplies to Azerbaijan exceeded US$832 million, creating a two-way agricultural relationship rather than a one-directional export channel. These established supply chains offer a practical area for stabilizing trade while larger industrial and infrastructure projects progress.
Russian Investment Rises Despite Weaker Merchandise Turnover
Moscow it appears has been listening to Azerbaijan’s perspective and has been making overtures to Baku. Investment figures provide a second measure of the relationship’s resilience. Russian direct investment in Azerbaijan reached US$237.119 million in the first half of 2026, up US$107.392 million, or 82.8%, from the same period of 2025. Russia accounted for 6.5% of all foreign direct investment entering Azerbaijan during the period. Azerbaijani investment in Russia moved in the opposite direction, reaching US$22.488 million in the first half, down US$5.85 million, or 20.6%, year on year. This difference illustrates an asymmetry in current capital flows: Russian investment into Azerbaijan is expanding while Azerbaijani investment into Russia has weakened. The longer-term corporate presence is considerable. Accumulated Russian investment in Azerbaijan has been reported at approximately US$10.7 billion, including US$2.9 billion in the non-oil economy. More than 1,400 Russian-capitalised companies were registered as active in Azerbaijan on April 1 this year. These businesses provide an existing platform for cooperation in manufacturing, distribution, services, energy and other commercial activities.
There has been a recent flurry of bilateral activity to get relations back on track. These include the September 26 meeting between Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak and Azerbaijani Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev in Baku, the October 5 intergovernmental talks in Moscow, and the October 9 trilateral Presidential meeting in Turkmenistan, a series of engagements has placed freight capacity, investment, energy cooperation and Caspian logistics at the centre of regional economic diplomacy.
The timing is significant. Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee puts bilateral trade at about US$2.4 billion in January-August 2026, compared with US$3.3 billion in the same period of 2025, a decline of about 27.3%. Yet Russian direct investment into Azerbaijan reached US$237.119 million in the first half of 2026, up 82.8% from US$129.727 million a year earlier. The combination suggests that the current adjustment is not simply a retreat from bilateral economic engagement. Rather, the composition of the relationship is changing, with investment and connectivity becoming more important relative to short-term merchandise turnover. The International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) is increasingly important to the relationship, linking Russian markets with Azerbaijan, Iran, India and wider South Asian destinations.
The September and October 2026 meetings therefore took place within an established business relationship rather than one dependent solely on government-level initiatives. The next task is to translate investment into additional production, trade and logistics capacity. Higher investment does not automatically compensate for declining exports, but it can create the industrial and commercial infrastructure required to rebuild trade over a longer period.
Transport & Investment Moves To The Centre Stage
Russia, Azerbaijan and Iran have intensified their economic and diplomatic engagement over the past two months, bringing bilateral trade, industrial cooperation, border infrastructure and regional transport connectivity into a common policy agenda. The meetings involved senior government officials in Baku and Moscow, business representatives, and the presidents of Russia, Azerbaijan and Iran, at CIS meetings held in Turkmenistan. Although the participants did not announce a new trilateral treaty or a quantified package of signed commercial contracts in the reported encounters, their discussions identified practical priorities for improving trade and developing regional transport infrastructure. The economic context is significant.
These figures point to an important distinction: short-term merchandise trade and longer-term economic integration are moving in different directions. The immediate challenge is to restore commercial turnover, particularly Russian exports to Azerbaijan, while preserving the investment, agricultural, energy and logistics links that support future growth. The INSTC provides a regional framework for addressing that challenge because its value extends beyond bilateral trade to freight movement between Russia and southern markets.
Alexander Novak & Shahin Mustafayev Review Economic Cooperation
On September 26, 2026, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak met Azerbaijani Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev in Baku to review cooperation in industry, energy, transport and logistics. Novak invited Azerbaijani counterparts to attend the Russian Energy Week in Moscow on October 14-16, creating a follow-up opportunity for discussions on energy projects, infrastructure and industrial cooperation.
The September meeting took place against the background of a substantial contraction in bilateral trade. The change was not evenly distributed between the two trading partners. Azerbaijan imported more than US$1.57 billion in goods from Russia, while Azerbaijani exports to Russia exceeded US$840 million.
Earlier figures reveal the direction of the adjustment. In January-June, bilateral turnover stood at US$1.728 billion, down 31.4% year on year. Azerbaijani exports to Russia increased 3% to US$608.557 million, whereas Russian exports to Azerbaijan declined 42% to US$1.120 billion. By January-July, turnover had reached US$2.110 billion, down 31.3%. Azerbaijani exports to Russia rose 3.9% to US$749.5 million, while imports from Russia fell 42.1% to US$1.36 billion.
Russia remained Azerbaijan’s third-largest source of imports after China and Türkiye in the first half of 2026, supplying 13.42% of the country’s imports. Russia also accounted for 12.33% of Azerbaijan’s non-oil exports in the January-July period, illustrating the Russian market’s importance to Azerbaijani producers even as overall trade weakened.
The figures suggest that the principal immediate problem is not a uniform collapse in demand. The sharper contraction in Russian exports points instead to a need to examine product-level competitiveness, supply arrangements, logistics, purchasing patterns and market access. For Azerbaijan, continued growth in exports to Russia helps sustain non-oil production. For Russia, recovering its position in the Azerbaijani market would help reverse the decline in bilateral turnover.

articles.full_text:
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited Uzbekistan on October 17–18, just ahead of United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrived in Samarkand on October 18 with a delegation of American business leaders seeking new contracts.
While China already has a substantial presence in Uzbek manufacturing and energy, Washington is seeking to expand American involvement in critical minerals and technology. The visits highlight the growing competition between the world’s two largest economies for influence in Central Asia.
On October 17, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev received Li Qiang. According to the Uzbek presidential administration, the portfolio of joint projects backed by firm agreements has reached nearly $60 billion. More than 6,000 joint ventures with Chinese participation have been established in Uzbekistan.
China is Uzbekistan’s largest trading partner. Bilateral trade totaled approximately $16–18 billion in 2025, according to Chinese and Uzbek figures. China accounted for 23% of Uzbekistan’s total foreign trade turnover in January–August 2026.
Railway Through Kyrgyzstan
Construction of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway was another topic of discussion. Work officially began in December 2024.
The route will cross mountainous areas of Kyrgyzstan and connect the railway networks of China and Uzbekistan. The 304-kilometer section through Kyrgyzstan alone is estimated to cost $4.7 billion and will require 50 bridges and 29 tunnels.
Uzbekistan is landlocked, making the cost and timing of its international freight shipments heavily dependent on transit conditions in neighboring countries. The railway through Kyrgyzstan will provide an additional route, reducing reliance on transit through Kazakhstan and potentially shortening journeys between China and Uzbekistan.
Beijing considers the railway part of its efforts to develop overland connections under the Belt and Road Initiative.
Rubio Arrives with American Business Delegation
On October 19, Rubio attended talks in Samarkand under the C5+1 format, bringing together the U.S. and Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.
Rubio said nearly 300 American businesses were represented in Samarkand. Companies were discussing agreements potentially worth billions of dollars, with concrete announcements expected following the meetings.
Among Washington’s priorities are critical minerals used in advanced technologies, including electronics and batteries.
The U.S. is seeking new sources of raw materials and opportunities to process them outside China. Beijing holds a dominant position in processing several of these materials, and American companies are interested in alternative suppliers.
Uzbekistan’s mineral deposits include copper and uranium. For Tashkent, an important question is whether American investment will bring new processing facilities and jobs or concentrate mainly on extracting and exporting raw materials.
Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Rubio said the U.S. was not asking Central Asian countries to end cooperation with other partners. Washington intends to compete for contracts and investment projects.
Chinese Enterprises and American Contracts
The gap between China and the U.S. is particularly stark in trade. According to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, American goods trade with Uzbekistan totaled just $1.05 billion in 2025, less than one-fifteenth of the value of Uzbekistan’s trade with China. Including services, U.S.–Uzbek trade reached approximately $1.7 billion.
Economic cooperation with the U.S. is developing through major investment projects, equipment supplies, financing, and technological partnerships.
In November 2025, during the C5+1 summit in Washington, Uzbekistan and the U.S. announced commercial agreements and contracts worth approximately $34.5 billion. President Donald Trump also spoke of planned Uzbek purchases and investments in the U.S. exceeding $100 billion over ten years.
Those announcements suggest considerable ambitions, but the trade figures show how far Washington remains behind Beijing.
Uzbekistan has long sought to maintain economic relationships with Western countries alongside its ties to China and Russia. Greater American investment would give Tashkent more options, but China’s commanding share of Uzbek trade illustrates how difficult it would be to reduce its dependence on Beijing.
Moreover, American and Chinese interests increasingly clash in sectors such as critical minerals and advanced technology. Washington wants to reduce its dependence on Chinese-controlled supply chains, while Beijing is expanding its own manufacturing and technological presence in Uzbekistan. Tashkent may welcome investment from both sides, but their competing priorities could complicate its efforts to work with them simultaneously.
Li Qiang’s visit demonstrated the depth of China’s existing economic ties with Uzbekistan. Rubio’s challenge is to turn Washington’s promises of investment into a commercial presence capable of narrowing the gap.

Foreign investors are looking outside Kazakhstan’s oil and gas sector. But turning that interest into investment will require predictable regulations and stronger cross-border connections, according to Saule Zhakayeva, chairperson of Citibank Kazakhstan’s management board and president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Kazakhstan (AmCham).
Citi has operated in Kazakhstan since 1994, when it opened a representative office in Almaty. In an interview with The Times of Central Asia, Zhakayeva discussed the country’s investment climate and its role as a regional business hub. She also addressed the future of economic relations between the United States and Kazakhstan.
TCA: How is foreign investor interest in Central Asia evolving, and which of Kazakhstan’s strengths are already translating into investment? Where do you see the strongest commercial opportunities over the next three to five years, and what would help turn untapped potential into committed capital?
Zhakayeva: Investors today are looking for markets that combine economic stability, access to natural resources, strategic geography, and long-term growth potential. Kazakhstan offers each of these attributes. The country has established itself as the largest economy in Central Asia, maintains a relatively strong institutional framework, and continues to pursue reforms aimed at improving the investment climate.
Most notably, investor interest is becoming increasingly diversified. Historically, foreign investment was concentrated primarily in oil and gas. Today, we see growing interest in transportation and logistics, renewable energy, critical minerals, digital infrastructure, financial services, manufacturing, and data-related investments.
This growing interest is also reflected in the increasing level of engagement between international investors and Kazakhstan. As President of the American Chamber of Commerce in Kazakhstan, I have seen firsthand the strong momentum in U.S.-Kazakhstan business relations. Throughout 2026, Kazakhstan has hosted a growing number of high-level business engagements involving senior representatives of American companies and institutions, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Business Mission to Kazakhstan and other executive-level dialogues focused on investment, trade, digital transformation, energy, and infrastructure.
AmCham Kazakhstan also led its first business delegation to Washington, D.C., bringing member companies together to strengthen bilateral economic ties, promote Kazakhstan’s investment opportunities, and advocate for deeper economic cooperation. These activities underscore the growing recognition of Kazakhstan and Central Asia as strategically important destinations for long-term investment and commercial cooperation.
More importantly, they are beginning to translate into tangible outcomes. For example, in 2026, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation announced plans to explore up to $700 million in financing opportunities to support the development of Kazakhstan’s critical minerals sector.
Kazakhstan’s location at the crossroads of Europe and Asia has become increasingly important as global companies diversify supply chains and seek alternative trade routes. The development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route is further strengthening Kazakhstan’s role in regional and global commerce, creating opportunities far beyond traditional sectors. Similar dynamics are being observed across the region, where alternative trade routes, logistics investments, and infrastructure development are becoming increasingly important to global investors.
We are also seeing growing international interest in strategic sectors linked to global energy security and the energy transition. Kazakhstan’s role as a major producer of uranium and its potential in critical minerals, renewable energy, and emerging green-energy value chains are attracting increasing international attention. These sectors are becoming increasingly important as governments and companies seek to diversify supply chains and secure access to strategic resources.
Looking ahead over the next three to five years, I believe the strongest opportunities will emerge in infrastructure, transport and logistics, the energy transition, critical minerals, digital economy initiatives, and sectors supporting regional trade.
To translate interest into committed capital, investors continue to value predictability. Continued progress in regulatory transparency, efficient infrastructure development, human capital, and cross-border connectivity will further strengthen Kazakhstan’s competitiveness.
TCA: Kazakhstan has faced repeated external shocks, including recent disruptions affecting global trade routes and financial markets. How do you assess its resilience, particularly in light of the recent sovereign rating upgrade to BBB by S&P Global Ratings and the country’s substantial financial buffers? Looking ahead, where do you see the main vulnerabilities, and what practical steps should companies take to mitigate financial and supply-chain risks?
Zhakayeva: Kazakhstan has demonstrated considerable resilience in navigating successive external shocks. Its macroeconomic fundamentals remain relatively strong, supported by substantial sovereign financial reserves, prudent fiscal management, and a diversified banking sector.
The recent upgrade of Kazakhstan’s sovereign credit rating to BBB by S&P is a significant milestone. Sovereign ratings are closely monitored by global investors because they provide an independent assessment of a country’s creditworthiness, policy credibility, and capacity to meet its financial obligations. The upgrade reflects confidence in Kazakhstan’s economic management, institutional framework, external balance sheet, and ability to maintain stability despite a challenging global environment.
We have observed this progress firsthand. Citi has served as an adviser to the Government of Kazakhstan on sovereign ratings since 2019, working closely with economic authorities to support engagement with international rating agencies and investors. During this period, Kazakhstan has achieved six sovereign rating upgrades, reflecting continued improvements in economic fundamentals, governance, and policy credibility. Today, Citi is also supporting discussions around a medium-term roadmap aimed at further strengthening Kazakhstan’s sovereign credit profile over time.
From an investment perspective, a stronger sovereign rating can help improve investor confidence, support access to international capital markets, and contribute to lower financing costs over time for both the public and private sectors. Combined with Kazakhstan’s substantial sovereign assets and financial buffers, it reinforces the country’s position as one of the stronger investment-grade markets in the region.
Investor engagement is equally important. As a committed financial partner to Kazakhstan for more than 30 years, Citi continues to help connect the country with global capital markets and international investors. Through investor forums, roadshows, and strategic dialogues in major financial centers such as New York and London, we help showcase Kazakhstan’s economic progress, reform agenda, and long-term investment potential to the global investment community.
At the same time, resilience today does not mean immunity. Businesses operate in an environment characterized by volatile commodity prices, changing trade patterns, geopolitical uncertainty, and fluctuating financial conditions. The most successful companies are responding by focusing on diversification. One of the key lessons emerging globally is that no company or country can rely on a single market, supplier, financing source, or trade route. Recent disruptions have reinforced the importance of building multiple channels for sourcing, logistics, and market access. Similar observations have been made regarding global supply chains and trade routes, where organizations increasingly seek alternatives rather than depending on a single corridor.
From a practical standpoint, companies should prioritize active foreign exchange risk management and hedging programs; diversification of funding sources and financing tenors; supply chain mapping and contingency planning; digital visibility across procurement and logistics networks; scenario planning to prepare for external disruptions.
Resilience is no longer simply about absorbing shocks. It is about maintaining strategic flexibility and being able to adapt quickly as circumstances evolve.
TCA: Kazakhstan is increasingly viewed as a commercial hub between Europe and Asia. Are you seeing more international companies establish regional headquarters in the country, and what factors are driving those decisions?
Zhakayeva: We increasingly see Kazakhstan recognized not only as an investment destination, but also as a regional operating hub. A growing number of international companies are evaluating Kazakhstan as a base from which to serve Central Asia and neighboring markets. Several factors are driving this trend.
First, Kazakhstan offers access to the largest economy in Central Asia and provides companies with a strategic platform for serving the wider region. Second, improvements in connectivity, logistics infrastructure, and trade corridors are making it easier for businesses to manage regional operations from Kazakhstan. Globally, companies are paying closer attention to jurisdictions that can serve as regional coordination centers for trade, finance, and supply chains. Third, Kazakhstan has developed a strong financial sector, a relatively deep talent pool, and an increasingly digital business environment.

By Patrick ReevellKevin ShalveyAnna Sergeeva,
1 days ago
LONDON and MOSCOW -- Ukraine overnight launched a massive aerial attack, sending hundreds of drones toward targets in Moscow and St. Petersburg, and striking a major oil terminal again despite pressure from President Donald Trump to end such attacks.
Drones struck a major oil terminal in St. Petersburg as well as a large data center, with videos posted online appearing to show fires burning. Video also appears to show a drone striking a huge bridge in the city.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said it had shot down some 1,015 drones near Moscow and several other western regions, making the attack one of the largest of the war. The attack also appeared to be the biggest St. Petersburg has witnessed.
St. Petersburg’s governor, Alexander Beglov, confirmed the attacks in the city, in a post on Telegram, writing, "Emergency services continue to work on extinguishing fires at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District."
One person was killed and five others were injured in St. Petersburg, Beglov said, saying that apartment buildings and homes had been damaged in the attack.
Two transformer substations were struck in Yanino, in the Leningrad region, Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said, adding that about 20,000 people were without electricity on Sunday morning. Russia media reported the attack was one of the largest the region had witnessed since the start of war.
Russia strikes power plant in Ukraine after Trump announces energy ceasefire
The strikes on the oil terminals also underline that Ukraine has returned to attacking Russia's oil industry after pausing to adhere to Trump's "energy ceasefire." The Kremlin never abided by that "ceasefire."
Ukraine had reluctantly halted the refinery attacks under pressure from Trump, after he announced last weekend that the two sides had agreed to the "ceasefire" and following his deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
It comes as Trump this week moved to further ease pressure on Putin while escalating it on Zelenskyy. Trump on Friday waived a sweeping new sanctions package passed by Congress. The sanctions law named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham would have significantly expanded measures targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry.
Trump signs order waiving Graham Act sanctions on Russia, drawing backlash from some lawmakers and Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy has criticised the move, saying it encourages Putin to keep fighting. He suggested on Saturday he believed Trump would likely move to further ease sanctions on Putin, saying the diesel deal was just the first step.
This week Ukraine also reported Elon Musk’s crucial Starlink internet system had been abruptly restricted on its drones, disrupting its military’s operations, with concerns in Kyiv the move was intended to further pressure it. There was also anxiety among officials in Ukraine that Trump may move to limit intelligence sharing providing warning about Russia missiles launches.
Russia has continued to heavily target Ukraine's energy infrastructure without pause despite Trump’s declaring the two sides had agreed to the "ceasefire" last weekend.
600,000 without power in Ukraine as Russia launches 'massive' attack amid Trump's 'energy ceasefire'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday morning accused Russia of "deliberately" launching at least 76 attacks on energy or oil and gas targets over the last week. He said Russia had launched attacks overnight on substations in four regions, including Odesa.
"Tens of thousands of families remain without power," Zelenskyy said on social media. "Energy workers and repair crews are working virtually around the clock to restore electricity supply."
Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight killed at least two people and injured at least a dozen others, he said.
Russia targets Ukraine with 'massive' aerial attack, including hundreds of drones, Zelenskyy says
"In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic," Zelenskyy said. "The main targets of these strikes are energy facilities -- the Russians are trying to cause a blackout. And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements."

articles.title: Uzbekistan Signs Space Accords as Rubio Opens Samarkand Talks - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Uzbekistan Signs Space Accords as Rubio Opens Samarkand Talks  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan joined the U.S.-led Artemis Accords on October 19 as Secretary of State Marco Rubio held talks in Samarkand. The signing accompanied the first Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue between the two countries, with critical minerals among the priorities.
Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov announced the signing after bilateral talks with Rubio. He said Uzbekistan had become the 77th country to join the framework for peaceful space exploration.
Saidov said accession would support closer cooperation with NASA and other participating space agencies. He identified training for Uzbek specialists and access to space technologies as potential benefits.
Established in 2020, the Artemis Accords set out principles for civilian space exploration. Signatories commit to peaceful operations and greater transparency, including sharing scientific data. The framework also addresses interference between missions and the preservation of historic sites in space. NASA describes the accords as nonbinding principles.
Posting on X, Rubio confirmed he had met all five Central Asian foreign ministers during the C5+1 gathering. He said cooperation would expand commercial opportunities and strengthen regional security. American businesses also joined the visit as Washington seeks deeper economic ties across Central Asia.
The visit follows the November 2025 White House summit, where Trump hosted all five Central Asian presidents. That meeting gave the partnership a stronger commercial focus, with aircraft orders and minerals projects featuring prominently. Samarkand brings ministers and businesses together to advance that agenda.
The strategic dialogue focused on implementing agreements reached by the countries’ leaders and expanding economic cooperation. Saidov said the discussions covered energy and advanced technologies, alongside critical minerals. Education and security cooperation were also on the agenda.
Rubio said separately that the talks addressed infrastructure and space cooperation, as well as engagement through C5+1, which brings together the United States and Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.
In a separate meeting with Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi, Rubio reaffirmed plans to expand economic and security cooperation. He thanked Kazakhstan for supporting “President Trump’s peace initiatives, including the Abraham Accords.”
Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Rubio said nearly 300 American businesses were represented, and that agreements potentially worth billions of dollars were under discussion. He presented the visit as the start of deeper U.S. economic engagement with Central Asia.
“I think we’ll have some concrete deals to announce,” he said, according to Euronews. A final list of agreements and their value had not been circulated at the time of those remarks.
Rubio identified critical minerals as a priority, arguing that concentrated supplies created risks for countries dependent on them. “This is not about coming here to say, stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country,” he said.
Days earlier, at the October 15 summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia in Baku, Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed a transport strategy spanning several international initiatives. His proposal included China’s Belt and Road and the planned Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) through Armenia. It illustrated the region’s pursuit of transport links involving different international partners, consistent with Rubio’s stated approach to U.S. engagement.
Samarkand also connects the current talks to the format’s origins. Following a proposal from Kazakhstan, John Kerry and the five Central Asian foreign ministers met in New York in September 2015 and again in Samarkand on November 1. The six governments initially focused on shared security concerns and economic connectivity, alongside environmental challenges. A secretariat followed in 2022, before Joe Biden hosted the first presidential-level meeting in New York in September 2023.
The 2023 summit also set the groundwork for a dedicated business platform and the Critical Minerals Dialogue, which began in February 2024. These initiatives widened cooperation beyond periodic diplomatic meetings, giving companies a more direct role in identifying investment opportunities and obstacles.
At the November 2025 summit, the U.S. Commerce Department announced more than $25 billion in commercial deals. Aviation formed a substantial part of the package, with Uzbekistan Airways ordering eight additional Boeing 787s, while Air Astana selected up to 15. The announcements also covered agricultural machinery and advanced computing, showing the breadth of U.S. commercial interest beyond mineral extraction. The package included firm orders alongside preliminary commitments.
The minerals discussions continued in Astana on June 10, when U.S. envoy Sergio Gor met officials from all five Central Asian countries. Sessions covered exploration and processing, with supply chain security central to Washington’s approach. Kazakhstan emphasized its interest in domestic processing and skilled jobs, seeking a larger industrial role than supplying raw materials alone.
Minerals cooperation already has a bilateral foundation. On February 4, Saidov and U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau signed a memorandum on supply chain security covering critical minerals and rare earth elements. It included both mining and processing.
Later that month, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation signed preliminary commercial terms for a joint investment framework with Uzbekistan. The proposed structure included a joint holding company intended to help develop investment projects.
The five countries have also developed their own regional consultation process, beginning with a leaders’ meeting in 2018. Their cooperation now extends to transport and energy, areas central to foreign investment. The region is pursuing parallel partnerships with China, the European Union, and other partners, giving the U.S. initiative a place within a broader expansion of Central Asia’s international economic ties.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in Uzbekistan with a delegation representing more than 200 American companies. He is attending a C5+1 ministerial meeting with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. The agenda includes regional connectivity, energy security, trade, private investment, and economic modernization.
The visit brings the format back to its birthplace. The first C5+1 ministerial meeting was held in Samarkand on November 1, 2015, with then-Secretary of State John Kerry.
The November 6, 2025, summit in Washington gave the relationship a substantial commercial dimension. Uzbekistan and the United States announced economic agreements and trade contracts worth approximately $34.5 billion. President Donald Trump also said Uzbekistan intended to purchase and invest more than $100 billion in the United States over the following decade.
Samarkand is now hosting a ministerial meeting accompanied by a large business delegation. The immediate question is how much of the previously announced portfolio has moved toward financing and implementation. In late September, Uzbekistan’s Minister of Investment, Industry, and Trade, Laziz Kudratov, valued the project portfolio with the United States at $35 billion, with approximately $7 billion already completed. On that accounting, about $28 billion remains.
In my assessment, the strongest overlap between American and Uzbek interests lies in processing critical minerals inside Uzbekistan, using American financing and technology to serve international supply chains. Washington wants alternative sources of strategic materials. Tashkent wants investment in industrial production rather than simply exporting raw materials.
Their positions are less closely aligned on technology and relations with Iran. Uzbekistan seeks access to American artificial intelligence infrastructure while maintaining cooperation with China. It also regards Iran as an important transit partner. Washington’s approach to sensitive technologies and sanctions could complicate both ambitions.
Another Uzbek priority is ending the application of the Jackson–Vanik Amendment to Uzbekistan, a U.S. trade-law provision dating from 1974 that continues to affect the legal framework for bilateral commerce. Rubio can support its repeal, but Congress must make the decision.
Investment Deals
The C5+1 format has become more commercially focused. At the Washington summit, the U.S. Department of Commerce organized a dedicated venue for business agreements and announced more than $25 billion in commercial deals involving the five Central Asian countries.
Since the Washington summit, Uzbekistan has developed additional channels for economic cooperation with the United States. A bilateral Business and Investment Council has brought together officials and business representatives. Cooperation has also expanded into critical minerals, energy, infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing.
In June 2026, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry, and Trade, its Fund for Reconstruction and Development, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), and the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) announced a joint investment platform.
Uzbekistan has also adopted a critical minerals development program for 2026–2030, covering 120 projects valued at $4.2 billion. The first stage includes 12 projects worth $166 million, with plans to produce high-purity selenium, tellurium, and rhenium.
These plans reflect Tashkent’s industrial priorities. Uzbekistan wants foreign partners to help build processing facilities and develop technological expertise, not merely purchase mineral concentrates.
The scale of American economic involvement still needs perspective. Bilateral trade exceeded $1 billion in 2025, while Uzbekistan’s total foreign trade turnover reached $81.2 billion. China remains a much larger trading partner for the region. The United States matters to Uzbekistan primarily as a potential source of long-term capital, advanced technology, and access to Western markets.
Critical Minerals, Transport, and the Middle Corridor
The agenda in Samarkand can be divided into six areas: critical minerals, transport, energy, trade rules, technology, and security.
Critical minerals are likely to attract particular attention. The February memorandum on cooperation in the sector and the June investment platform provide a basis for negotiations, but project financing and processing arrangements remain decisive.
Kazakhstan offers an example of the type of transaction Washington is pursuing. U.S.-based Cove Capital is involved in a tungsten project, and EXIM has issued a nonbinding letter of interest for financing of up to $900 million.
Transport is another regional priority. The Middle Corridor connects Central Asia to Europe through the Caspian Sea and South Caucasus. Washington has also supported the development of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a proposed transport connection through Armenia.
These routes offer the United States alternatives to transit through Russia and Iran. For Central Asian countries, the practical concern is access to ports, railways, and markets through several directions.
Energy cooperation could cover electricity grids, renewable power, and nuclear regulation. Trade discussions are likely to include Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the future of the Jackson–Vanik Amendment.
Technology presents a more difficult set of questions. Uzbekistan wants access to American chips, cloud infrastructure, and AI models while also benefiting from lower-cost Chinese technology. Its interest in the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative must be understood against that broader policy.
Security discussions may involve Afghanistan and sanctions compliance. Iran could also arise in bilateral talks, particularly because Uzbek transport planners see Iranian territory as a route to southern ports.
What Washington Wants from Central Asia
For the United States, critical minerals are an immediate strategic concern. Washington is seeking to diversify supply chains in sectors where China plays a dominant role, especially processing. Central Asia has substantial deposits of uranium, tungsten, antimony, and other strategic materials. Uzbekistan’s copper and uranium resources make it a potential partner.
American companies are also interested in aviation, industrial equipment, services, and finance. During the November 2025 summit, Uzbekistan Airways increased its firm Boeing 787 order to 22 aircraft, illustrating how commercial transactions have become part of the administration’s diplomacy toward the region.
Washington’s technological interests extend beyond mineral extraction. Advanced semiconductors, cloud services, and sensitive digital infrastructure have become areas of competition with China. Uzbekistan’s effort to work with both countries may require careful negotiation over technology access and restrictions.
Nuclear energy deserves attention as well. Uzbekistan is pursuing a nuclear power project involving Russia while also expanding regulatory contacts with the United States. Cooperation on nuclear safety does not, by itself, indicate a change in the project’s principal partners.
Nor has Washington publicly demanded that Central Asian states withdraw from the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, abandon cooperation with the Eurasian Economic Union, or cancel existing Russian nuclear projects.
American diplomacy toward Uzbekistan also relies on personal relationships. The bilateral Business and Investment Council has established a channel involving senior Uzbek officials and U.S. representatives, including Sergio Gor. Such contacts may accelerate negotiations, but major financing decisions still depend on the relevant institutions, while changes to U.S. trade law require congressional approval.
What Tashkent Wants in Return
For Uzbekistan, the central objective is to secure investment on terms that support domestic industrial development. American government financing could help attract private investors to projects that would otherwise be difficult to fund.
Technology is equally important. Uzbek officials have expressed interest in both American computing infrastructure and Chinese open-source AI models. The country’s ambitions in artificial intelligence depend on access to computing capacity, reliable electricity, and skilled personnel.
Local processing is the third priority. Under Uzbekistan’s minerals program, new investment is intended to increase the value of products manufactured domestically. Whether American participation supports that objective will depend on the ownership structure, technology transfer, and processing requirements of individual projects.
The fourth priority is trade-law reform.
The Jackson–Vanik Amendment continues to create uncertainty in Uzbekistan’s commercial relationship with the United States. Rubio described it as an obstacle during a Senate appearance in June 2026 and expressed support for lifting the restrictions. But legislative proposals have repeatedly failed to become law.
Uzbekistan’s WTO accession adds urgency to the issue. Bilateral market-access negotiations with the United States were completed in December 2024. Tashkent wants a stable trade relationship backed by legislation rather than arrangements that require periodic renewal.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio landed in Samarkand, Uzbekistan on Sunday evening to begin a tour that includes Central Asia and India, and the trip is framed as his first stop in a broader effort to strengthen trade ties and counter Russia and China’s influence. Rubio arrived at the head of a delegation of more than 200 business leaders to attend a ministerial meeting of the C5+1 group, which includes the United States and the Muslim-majority states that were part of the Soviet Union: Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. Kazakhstan has become the first country in Central Asia to join the World Bank Group's global Metals and Minerals Compact initiative. The Compact's strategy, developed by Kazakhstan's Ministry of Industry and Construction and the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms in cooperation with the World Bank, aims to help mobilize around $20 billion in investment by 2031. Achieving this target will depend on preparing specific projects, creating favorable conditions for investors, and developing the necessary infrastructure.
The scale of the task reflects the importance of the mining and metals sector to Kazakhstan's economy. Mining remains the largest single block of Kazakhstan’s industry. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, industrial output in January–September 2026 totaled 51.9 trillion tenge (about $109.3 billion). Mining and quarrying, which in official statistics includes oil and gas, accounted for 24.4 trillion tenge ($51.3 billion), or 46.9%
The mining sector's substantial share of industrial output reflects its role in Kazakhstan's economy. However, the economic returns from mineral resources depend not only on extraction volumes but also on how much raw material is processed domestically and how much value this processing generates. Ore beneficiation, deeper processing, and the production of higher-value-added goods can help develop new manufacturing activities, create demand for equipment, engineering and transport services, and expand opportunities for local suppliers.
Developing domestic processing requires not only investment but also favorable conditions for implementing projects. Industrial facilities need reliable energy supplies, transport infrastructure, modern technologies, and skilled workers. Reliable geological data, transparent licensing procedures, and predictable regulation are equally important. When information about mineral reserves is insufficient, investors find it more difficult to assess the prospects of deposits. Uncertainty over the rules governing operations can also increase risks and extend project timelines.
Cooperation with the World Bank could help Kazakhstan identify the necessary reforms, improve conditions for investors, and prepare projects to attract capital. However, the outcome will depend on the extent to which the proposed measures translate into concrete regulatory changes and better conditions for implementing investment projects.
The development of critical mineral processing is also being pursued through individual investment projects in Kazakhstan. One example is a tungsten processing plant project worth more than $1.1 billion involving US-based Cove Capital in the Karaganda region. It illustrates interest in establishing facilities focused on processing mineral raw materials. However, the actual economic impact will depend on the project's implementation, its production capacity, and its ability to manufacture competitive products.
At the same time, expanding extraction and processing entails environmental and social risks. Industrial facilities may consume significant amounts of water and electricity, place additional pressure on the environment, and affect local communities. Environmental and social requirements therefore need to be taken into account at the project preparation stage. This is important not only for sustainable development but also for assessing risks that could affect implementation timelines and financing terms.
The effectiveness of the World's Bank Metals and Minerals Compact should be assessed by the volume of investment actually mobilized, the launch of new processing facilities, and an increase in the share of higher-value-added products in exports. The creation of skilled jobs and the development of local supply chains are equally important.
Ultimately, the success of the partnership will depend not only on whether Kazakhstan manages to attract the targeted $20 billion by 2031, but also on whether this investment leads to new production facilities, expanded processing capacity, and a higher share of value-added products in exports. These outcomes will show whether the country can generate greater economic returns from its mineral resources and strengthen its position in international production chains.

This article explains these development dynamics and is essential reading for anyone involved in Russian and ASEAN affairs.
The immediate Russian trade and investment opportunities are visible across Southeast Asia. Vietnam recorded US$4.77 billion in bilateral trade with Russia in 2025, while Indonesia’s trade approached US$5 billion. Li said that China is ready to work with Uzbekistan to further leverage the complementary strengths of the two economies, continuously enhance connectivity in infrastructure, finance and other areas, advance the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway and strive for more tangible outcomes.
China is also willing to import more high-quality and specialty products from Uzbekistan and welcomes Uzbekistan to make full use of platforms such as the China International Import Expo to actively explore the Chinese market, he added.
Li encouraged the two sides to continue to make good use of the mutual visa exemption policy, expand two-way personnel exchanges, strengthen exchanges and cooperation in culture, tourism, education, youth, locality and other fields, and constantly enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the two peoples.
China stands ready to strengthen coordination and cooperation with Uzbekistan within multilateral frameworks such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the China-Central Asia mechanism and the United Nations, work with all parties to implement the four global initiatives, and advance an equal and orderly multipolar world and a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, he said.
For his part, Aripov said that Uzbekistan admires China's remarkable achievements in development and sincerely appreciates China's strong support for Uzbekistan's reform and development efforts.
Under the joint guidance of the two heads of state, Uzbekistan-China relations have continued to reach new heights, he noted.
Aripov said that Uzbekistan is willing to work with China to fully promote the construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway and other Belt and Road cooperation projects, deepen mutually beneficial cooperation in economic and trade investment, agriculture, energy and mineral resources, customs, finance, digital technology, artificial intelligence, ecological protection and other fields, strengthen exchanges in tourism, education, locality and other fields, enhance multilateral coordination, and promote the continued development of the Uzbekistan-China all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era.
Before the talks, the two leaders jointly watched a video showcasing practical cooperation between China and Uzbekistan across various fields.
