articles.title: Rubio Travels To Central Asia As US Seeks Deeper Trade And Security Ties In Region - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.summary: Rubio Travels To Central Asia As US Seeks Deeper Trade And Security Ties In Region  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in Samarkand to meet the leaders and foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan for several days of high-level diplomatic engagement that Washington hopes will translate into concrete economic and security cooperation.
Asked by a reporter before departing Joint Base Andrews why he was traveling to Central Asia amid multiple international crises, Rubio said the visit was about strengthening relationships rather than responding to a single emergency.
He said the dates had been chosen to accommodate all five leaders and foreign ministers, stressing that immediate crises should not eclipse longer-term diplomatic priorities.
"One of the things that suffers is the strategic business," Rubio said, describing how crisis-driven diplomacy can push other important relationships aside.
He cited recent trips to Greece and Latin America as part of the administration's effort to maintain partnerships beyond the most urgent international disputes.
Central Asia is strategically positioned between Europe and Asia, and its governments maintain important economic, security and diplomatic ties with both Russia and China. The region also has significant energy and mineral resources.
For Washington, closer engagement offers an opportunity to expand cooperation with countries seeking to balance their relationships with major powers.
Rubio said the trip reflected the need to invest in those partnerships even as the war in Ukraine, pressure on energy markets, and tensions involving Iran continue to dominate the international agenda.
Diplomacy And Trade
Speaking to reporters on a background call on October 16 Rubio's visit, a State Department official said more than 200 American companies would accompany the secretary to Samarkand, where he is expected to meet with the foreign ministers of all five Central Asian countries.
The tour reflects the Trump administration's effort to combine diplomacy with trade, investment, and security cooperation across South and Central Asia.
"For too long, the United States has focused on the Middle East and the East, and this area in the middle, Central Asia, has not gotten the attention that it deserves," the senior official said.
The American delegation will include representatives of major companies such as Boeing, Citibank, and Franklin Templeton, as well as businesses operating in critical minerals and other strategic sectors.
Officials from the US International Development Finance Corporation, the Export-Import Bank of the United States, the National Security Council, and the State Department will also participate in meetings designed to connect American businesses with potential partners across Central Asia.
The senior State Department official said Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan alone had generated more than $30 billion in new investments into the United States over the past year.
Republican Senator John Curtis, who has supported closer US engagement with Central Asia, says the region's stability is essential to American interests at a time of heightened uncertainty elsewhere in the world.
"A stable Central Asian region, with so much uncertainty in other parts of the globe, is just essential for us," he told RFE/RL.
"It's up to them, but to partner with us could be an incredibly important part of a relationship. As everybody knows, critical minerals are very important, not just to the United States but to the world. And I think that's a great asset they have that could be very important."
Samarkand, a historic trading center on the Silk Road, will serve as the main venue for the Central Asian portion of Rubio's trip.
The visit will include bilateral meetings and the C5+1 format meeting, as well as direct engagement between American companies, regional businesses, and government representatives.
Kazakhstan's announced intention to join the Abraham Accords was another key development highlighted during the briefing. The senior official said Washington was working toward a potential signing ceremony but did not provide a date.
“Stay tuned," the official said, adding that the sides hoped to complete the process "sooner than later."
The Abraham Accords were originally established to normalize relations between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority countries.
Kazakhstan's potential participation would extend the framework's reach, although the official did not provide details about the terms or timing of the country's formal accession.
The official also said Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan had been invited to attend the Group of 20 summit as observers for the first time.
The invitations were presented as part of Washington's broader effort to raise Central Asia's international profile and deepen ties with its governments.
All five Central Asian presidents have publicly invited US President Donald Trump to visit their countries, the official said, adding that regional governments had welcomed Washington's increased engagement.
Trade and investment are not the only priorities. The United States is also looking to strengthen counterterrorism cooperation with some Central Asian countries.
The official did not identify the countries involved or provide details of the initiatives but described security cooperation as an important element of Washington's expanding regional relationships.
The renewed outreach comes as Central Asian governments maintain complex relationships with Russia and China while seeking to broaden their international partnerships.
The official did not describe the initiative as an effort to displace either power, instead emphasizing commercial opportunities, stronger diplomatic contacts, and cooperation on shared security concerns.
Rubio's visit is intended to turn the outcomes of that high-level engagement into practical cooperation.
Following the Uzbekistan visit, Rubio is scheduled to travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar, India, to advance economic and diplomatic ties with New Delhi.

articles.title: Rubio focuses on trade routes and critical minerals in Central Asia - Euronews
articles.summary: Rubio focuses on trade routes and critical minerals in Central Asia  Euronews
articles.full_text:
The US and five Central Asian governments backed closer transport and industrial cooperation at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand. Rubio also held bilateral talks, while Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries agreed to deepen cooperation on transport, critical minerals and security at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand on Monday.
The talks brought together the United States, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In a joint statement, they backed investment in the Trans-Caspian trade route, closer industrial cooperation and simpler customs procedures.
A trade route to Europe
The Trans-Caspian route, also known as the Middle Corridor, connects Central Asia with European markets through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey, bypassing Russia.
"We're going to enhance the infrastructure of the Trans Caspian trade route and give our partners more ways to reach American and Central Asian markets," Rubio said.
Washington also wants to diversify supplies of critical minerals used in energy technologies and advanced manufacturing. The six governments identified mineral processing, energy cooperation and cybersecurity among their priorities, but the joint statement gave no figures for new infrastructure funding.
Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov proposed cooperation extending from mineral exploration to processing and local industrial clusters. He also called for closer links between the C5+1 diplomatic forum and the B5+1 business platform to involve companies in identifying projects.
The US push comes as the five Central Asian states maintain extensive economic ties with Russia and China. Speaking separately to Euronews in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington was seeking competition, not exclusivity.
"This is not about coming here to say, stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country," he told Euronews.
Bilateral talks with the five ministers
Rubio also held separate meetings with each of his Central Asian counterparts.
Kazakhstan's Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi discussed trade, energy, critical minerals and technology with Rubio. Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry said the US Secretary of State expressed interest in visiting the country after the G20 summit in Miami in December, although no date was announced.
The US State Department said they also discussed Kazakhstan's commitment to join the Abraham Accords, a US-backed framework for normalising relations with Israel.
Rubio also met Kyrgyzstan's Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev to discuss bilateral cooperation. Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin raised trade, investment and regional security, according to his ministry.
Rubio held talks with Turkmenistan's Rashid Meredov, with the two countries preparing another round of political consultations in Ashgabat in November.
Uzbekistan and the US held the first session of their Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue, covering trade, energy, technology and security. Following the talks, Foreign Minister Saidov signed the Artemis Accords in Rubio's presence, making Uzbekistan the 77th country to join the international framework for peaceful space exploration.

articles.title: Rubio’s visit to Central Asia boosts trade ties - Eurasianet
articles.summary: Rubio’s visit to Central Asia boosts trade ties  Eurasianet
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan in recent days has served as an octagon of competition between the United States and China over economic influence in Central Asia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio led an almost 300-strong American business delegation to the Uzbek city of Samarkand for a business forum, where on October 19, he held talks with the foreign ministers from all five Central Asian states.
Uzbek media, citing the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, reported that the trip yielded at least 54 business deals worth $12 billion, covering such areas as industry, transport and energy infrastructure, critical minerals, the financial sector, digital technologies, agriculture, healthcare, and education.
A joint statement by the participating foreign ministers outlined intentions to strengthen US-Central Asian ties in a variety of areas. Curiously, the document did not specifically reference artificial intelligence or critical minerals, two priority areas for the Trump administration. It did, however, “envision expanded opportunities for mineral extraction.”
The United States pledged to help Central Asia fulfill “its export potential by developing innovative ways to increase value-added products within the region and [create] pathways to introduce these products to the international market,” the statement noted. “By leveraging secure and trusted technology, American technological excellence, and the growing technology sectors of Central Asia, we seek to foster a region where e-commerce flourishes, innovative solutions abound, and talented entrepreneurs thrive.”
President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on October 19 held meet-and-greets with several US executives, including Rafael Santana, the CEO of locomotive-maker Wabtec, and Jenny Johnson, CEO of the asset management firm Franklin Templeton.
One of the agreements announced in Samarkand involves a Wabtec initiative to localize production of railway equipment. Meanwhile, Franklin Templeton, along with other finance firms including Oppenheimer & Co., Citigroup and BlackRock, will help Uzbek companies widen access to global capital markets.
The deals mark a significant step forward for US-Central Asian trade relations. Prior to the Samarkand meetings, there had been lots of hopeful talk about improving trade ties since President Trump’s return to office in January 2025. But the talk seemed to be out-pacing actual US dealmaking – at least until now.
Just a day before Rubio’s arrival in Uzbekistan, Mirziyoyev met in Tashkent with Li Qiang, China’s prime minister. Mirziyoyev’s statement touted Tashkent’s close relationship with Beijing.
“Both sides welcomed the active dialogue and cooperation at the parliamentary, governmental, ministerial, regional and business levels,” Mirziyoyev stated. He went on to emphasize the steady growth of bilateral trade. “The portfolio of projects backed by firm agreements has reached nearly $60 billion, and more than 6,000 joint ventures have been established so far,” he added.
China’s volume of trade with Central Asian states, given the advantage of geographic proximity, dwarfs that of the United States. The US and Uzbekistan exchanged an estimated $1.7 billion in goods and services in 2025. Uzbek-Chinese trade turnover reached almost $18 billion the same year, according to Uzbek government data.
The timing of Li’s visit could be seen as an attempt to upstage Rubio’s arrival, geopolitical gamesmanship akin to a surprise US diplomatic visit to Bishkek by Sergio Gor, Trump’s Special Envoy for South and Central Asia, and retiring Montana Sen. Steve Daines in early September that disrupted a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit. The headline of a South China Morning Post account of Li’s trip read: “China moves to cement ties with Uzbekistan amid tussle with US for Central Asian influence.”
In Samarkand, Rubio indicated that the United States is playing catch-up to China. “We have products, we have companies. … And we just want fair competition and an opportunity,” he said during his press briefing. “There’s no part of the world in which we feel like America and American business should not be – have a fair shot to compete, and that’s what we seek to do.”
Over the summer, the State Department floated a trial balloon that, in effect, sought to force Central Asian states to make a clear choice between cooperating with the United States or China on AI development. Central Asian leaders flatly rejected the idea.
Rubio in Samarkand stressed that the United States was not striving to force Central Asian states to choose between Washington and Beijing. He maintained his visit was “not about coming here to say stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country.”

articles.title: Marco Rubio Sees Central Asia as Promising Investment Hub - UzDaily.uz
articles.summary: Marco Rubio Sees Central Asia as Promising Investment Hub  UzDaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Central Asian countries could jointly attract investment, develop trade partnerships and secure the resources needed to strengthen their sovereignty and improve prosperity. He made the remarks at a C5+1 meeting of foreign ministers from the United States and Central Asian countries.
“Together, we can provide our countries with the resources, investments, opportunities and trade partnerships needed to ensure that each of our countries remains sovereign and that we collectively increase our shared prosperity,” Rubio said.
According to Rubio, the C5+1 format reflects Washington’s interest in strengthening peaceful relations with Central Asian states and its commitment to further developing cooperation.
He stressed that the United States seeks to protect critical industries and the supply chains that support them, reducing dependence on unreliable foreign partners and preserving economic independence. He described Central Asia as a promising destination for investment and exports, as well as an important source of materials needed for the future development of countries worldwide.
Among the practical areas of cooperation, Rubio highlighted the modernisation of transport infrastructure along the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, expanding regional companies’ access to US and Central Asian markets, and developing integrated, high-value-added supply chains for critical minerals.
Washington also intends to support training for specialists working with advanced US technologies. Rubio said the effort would involve preparing thousands of young professionals for Central Asia’s growing technology sector.
He identified the B5+1 business forum as another tool for expanding economic ties, saying it should promote dialogue between governments and businesses and increase mutual trade and investment.
Rubio also recalled the C5+1 meeting held in Washington last year. According to him, the event at the White House resulted in new deals worth US$25 billion, strengthening transport, energy, finance and other key sectors of the participating economies.
Rubio said US President Donald Trump and Central Asian leaders had agreed at the time to establish regulatory frameworks and labour market rules conducive to trade and investment. The current meetings, he added, are intended to advance the implementation of those commitments.
Concluding his remarks, Rubio emphasised that all Central Asian countries are independent states with their own cultures and interests and the right to determine their futures. The United States wants to see them prosper and is ready to act as a partner in that process.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president. Mirziyoyev received a Chinese delegation led by Li, who conveyed greetings and best wishes from Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The two sides discussed ways to strengthen their comprehensive strategic partnership and implement agreements reached by Mirziyoyev and Xi during their meeting in Bishkek in August 2026.
Priority areas for expanded cooperation include renewable energy, chemicals, geology, automotive manufacturing, metallurgy, agriculture, infrastructure modernization, the peaceful use of nuclear energy, digital technologies, artificial intelligence, machine-tool manufacturing and robotics.
The leaders also reviewed progress on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, a strategic regional transport project currently under construction. Its launch is expected to strengthen trade links and improve transport connectivity across Central Asia.
Additionally, the discussions covered efforts to expand tourism, cultural and educational exchanges. The two countries are considering increasing flight frequencies between their cities, while Uzbekistan Culture Days are scheduled to take place in China. Both sides also plan to open cultural centers in each other’s countries.
The talks reaffirmed Uzbekistan’s support for the One China policy and addressed cooperation within multilateral frameworks, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Central Asia-China format.
The meeting builds on expanding economic ties between the two countries. In August 2026, Mirziyoyev and Xi discussed raising bilateral trade to $30 billion in the coming years, alongside broader investment and industrial cooperation.
China is a major economic partner for Uzbekistan, with cooperation spanning energy, transport, manufacturing and technology. The railway project is expected to further strengthen regional connectivity and support trade flows between China and Central Asia.
